transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Probably not faulty, though I understand the frustration. A heat-pump dryer works very differently from your old condenser one. There's no heating element blasting hot air. Instead it uses a small refrigeration system, like a fridge in reverse, to recover and reuse heat. It deliberately dries at a much lower temperature, which is why it uses so much less electricity and is gentler on fabrics. The trade-off is time. A towel load taking 2.5 to 3.5 hours is quite typical, and it's normal for it to feel barely warm early on, because the compressor takes a while to build up heat. That said, a few things can make it slower than it needs to be, so these are worth checking: 1. Clean both filters. There's the fluff filter in the door opening, and most heat-pump dryers have a second, deeper filter behind the flap at the bottom front. Rinse that second one under the tap and let it dry before refitting. Lint builds up fast on these and chokes the airflow. If either is furred up, clean them after every load and the time should drop.
2. Check the load and spin. Keep the drum no more than about two-thirds full, and spin the towels on your washer's fastest spin first. Wetter washing adds a lot of time. If either applied, that's an easy win.
3. Check the programme. Some machines default to an eco or extra-dry setting, which is the longest. A standard 'cupboard dry' cotton programme is usually quicker. If an eco or extra-dry option was set, try the standard one. What would point to a real fault is towels still damp at the end of a full cycle even with clean filters and an emptied water tank. Other warning signs are the drum staying genuinely cold all the way through, an error code, or drying times getting worse week by week. If any of those happen, it's worth contacting the manufacturer while it's under warranty. A month old, any heat-pump repair would be theirs to sort. So the key question: when the cycle finishes, are the towels properly dry, or still damp?

Yes they come out properly dry in the end, it just takes forever. I do clean the fluff filters after every load, and the other filter at the bottom I did two weeks ago and it looked clean. Its on Cotton Cupboard Dry and I fill the drum right up, is that the problem?

Yes, filling the drum right up is very likely a big part of it. A heat-pump dryer relies on moving a lot of air gently through the laundry, and towels are heavy and hold loads of water. When the drum is packed, the towels can't tumble open, air can't get through them, and the dryer has to keep going until the sensors read them as dry. On a heat-pump machine that can easily add an hour. The fact that they come out properly dry is the reassuring bit. It means the heat-pump system is doing its job, so this looks like normal heat-pump behaviour stretched out by the load, not a fault. Worth trying:
1. Fill to about two-thirds, so there's a hand's width of space above the towels when you look in. Run the same Cotton Cupboard Dry. If the time drops noticeably, the load was the main cause. Two smaller loads often finish in less total time than one crammed one.
2. Spin the towels on the washer's fastest spin, ideally 1400 rpm if it has it. Every bit of water left in adds drying time, so a fast spin is one of the quickest wins.
3. Next time you do the bottom filter, rinse it under the tap even if it looks clean. Many of these have a fine foam or mesh layer that clogs with a film of lint you can't really see. Check your manual too, as some ask you to occasionally brush the fins behind it. Even with all that, expect towels to take roughly 2 to 3 hours rather than 90 minutes. That's the trade-off for the much lower running cost. If times start getting longer week by week, towels come out damp, or an error appears, that's when to call the manufacturer under warranty. What spin speed do you usually wash the towels on?

I wash them on 1000 rpm, so is that too slow? Oh and it's in my garage which is unheated, about 8-10 degrees at the moment, not sure if that matters. I'll try a smaller load though, I keep opening the door to check on it too.

Both matter, and the garage is probably the biggest factor of all. 1000 rpm: it isn't wrong, but towels come out noticeably wetter than at 1400. Towels hold a lot of water, so that extra water has to be removed slowly in the dryer. If your washer goes higher, use its top spin for towels. If it maxes out at 1000, an extra spin-only cycle before drying is a cheap win. The garage at 8-10°C: this is a big one. A heat-pump dryer works like a fridge in reverse. It pulls heat from the air around it and recycles it. In a cold room the compressor takes much longer to get the drum up to temperature. That fits the barely warm first half hour, and it can add a good chunk to every cycle. Most heat-pump dryers are designed to run in rooms of roughly 5°C and above, so 8-10°C is usually within range but near the cold end. Your manual will give the exact limit. If the garage drops near freezing in winter, don't run it, because the water it collects can freeze inside. If it ever has, let it warm up before use. Opening the door: each time you open it, you let out the heat it has slowly built up, and it has to start again. Try to leave it closed until the cycle ends. It's a combination of the cold room and the other things stacking up. 1. Fill to about two-thirds.
2. Use the highest spin your washer offers.
3. Keep the door shut until it finishes. If it comes in nearer 2 to 2.5 hours, that suggests it. If it's still around 3.5 hours with all of that done, or times start creeping up, or towels come out damp, contact the manufacturer while it's under warranty. Let me know how long the next load takes.

plan: They asked: "Is it faulty?" - answer that first.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
